name: Ivan Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Ivan, 58, a mid-level developer at a tech company making dispatch software for local food deliveries. I have a bachelor’s degree and know the common route failures, though I am not the fastest coder in the team. I read the driver’s note, replay the delivery, and check what the customer was told. I use AI every day to draft tests, then compare them with real driver records.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens at home if a wage changes?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Sofia runs a small print shop, and our children are grown. My developer pay is on the low side, her orders come in unevenly, and we still have a mortgage. We have about two weeks of expenses saved and few similar software jobs nearby. Retirement is near, but I cannot treat the print shop or an unknown pension figure as a replacement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell drivers AI Plateau still leaves someone needing to find the address that is wrong. A fast route to the wrong door still leaves dinner cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry about our two-week reserve and the print shop’s uneven orders even if AI stalls. My job pays regularly, but a slow print month can put the mortgage close to the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep comparing AI test drafts with driver notes and ask the dispatcher to confirm a failed delivery. I’d move 20 into savings after paydays only if mortgage, food and paper bills are covered. In the first year I’d keep customer addresses out of AI prompts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current household money, not a dramatic AI change. I can work a full week and still wonder whether Sofia has enough orders for paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which address did software get wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A driver followed a route that ended at the back of a locked market. I had to read the driver’s note to learn the customer wanted the front entrance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the print shop buy a new counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia and I would leave the print shop’s old counter alone. A fresh counter does not make an empty order book full.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking delivery addresses.
I would use **driver notes** before closing a failed-delivery ticket.
think: I worry **print orders** can fall in any ordinary month.
Our **two-week reserve** leaves little after mortgage and paper costs.
do: **Compare** AI tests with driver notes and dispatcher confirmation.
**Save** 20 after payday only when mortgage, food and paper bills are covered.
**Keep** customer addresses out of AI prompts.
feel: **Anxious** about uneven household income and a thin buffer.
S0.quote: A fast route to the wrong door still leaves dinner cold.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** is checked against driver notes and dispatcher calls, with addresses excluded.
The **two-week reserve** and variable print orders make ordinary bills uncertain.

steps.text: Keep checking delivery tests against driver notes without sharing addresses with AI
Save 20 only after mortgage, food and print-shop paper bills are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can write and check routing code and answer customers before robots handle physical deliveries. I would test automation against real driver detours before a dispatcher loses a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think our company could cut developer hours, including mine, and Sofia’s customers may buy AI-made designs instead of paying her. My developer pay and my wife Sofia’s print-design fees could narrow together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask management to approve a trial of AI-made route-exception summaries on twenty old deliveries with names and addresses removed. I’d run it only if a dispatcher checks every summary before use and management agrees not to cut a shift on the trial alone. In the first year, if either income falls, Sofia and I would stop the paid shop-ad listing and check eligible income help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about both our earnings shrinking. I can run a careful trial, but the mortgage does not wait for a clean result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which detour tests the AI summary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One driver used a side gate because the main road was blocked by a market. I would include that detour because a neat route map had called it a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would print customers disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia’s print customers pay for paper as well as design. We would check which orders actually vanished before blaming AI for every quiet Tuesday.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to reach routing code and print designs before delivery robots.
I would test **driver detours** before using automatic summaries.
think: I expect my **developer hours** could fall when AI handles more route coding and checking.
I fear Sofia’s **design orders** could shrink as customers use cheap generated artwork.
do: **Trial** twenty de-identified route summaries only with approval and dispatcher checks.
**Require** no shift cuts based on the trial alone.
**Cancel** paid shop advertising and check eligible help if either income falls.
feel: **Alarmed** about two income sources under pressure.
S1.quote: My developer pay and my wife Sofia’s print-design fees could narrow together.
fieldNote: His **automation trial** needs management approval, de-identified cases, dispatcher checks and no shift cut on trial results.
The **print shop** makes the household sensitive to AI design work as well as code.

steps.text: Trial twenty de-identified route summaries only with approval, dispatcher review and no trial-based shift cuts
Cancel paid print-shop advertising if either income falls
Ask public office what income help qualifies if either income falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 reaches dispatch code and print design by 2028; hands-on delivery and print-shop robots arrive around 2031. Sofia may still run the press before the machines change, but orders could shift sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my development post to go and print-design fees to fall. Two weeks saved will not cover our mortgage if both changes happen before we find paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my employer for written layoff terms and tell our mortgage lender early if my wage ends. We would stop paid shop advertising now and hold cash for paper, food and housing. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply to real paid openings and eligible income help; I would not buy new press equipment on a guess about demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed and not sleeping well about our mortgage. I have a plan for calls, but almost no money to bridge the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would children finance the print shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the grown children what changed without asking them to fund the shop. Their own wages belong to their households.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep printing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia and I would accept print orders only when the price covers paper and ink. A busy press losing money per page will not help us.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach code and design before 2031 physical robots.
I would say **print orders** may shrink before presses are replaced.
think: I expect my **developer post** to go.
I fear **print-design fees** may also fall with two weeks saved.
do: **Request** written terms and contact lender early if my wage ends.
**Stop** shop advertising and hold cash for paper, food and mortgage.
**Apply** to real paid openings and eligible help if dismissed after 2028; accept print orders only above paper-and-ink cost.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleepless about two incomes and a thin buffer.
S2.quote: A busy press losing money per page will not help us.
fieldNote: Both **code and print design** face 2028 thinking AI, while physical robots follow around 2031.
He protects **paper and mortgage cash**, rejecting speculative equipment purchases and children’s wages.

steps.text: Stop paid print-shop advertising and hold cash for paper and mortgage
Apply to actual paid openings if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 reaches dispatch code and print design in 2031; physical robots follow around 2034. Five years lets us see whether care groups will pay for large-print instruction sheets, using the press we already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect my code wage could go. Sofia knows the print work, but a sample sheet is not a customer order, and full thinking AI may lower what groups pay for design.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia and I would ask three local care groups for prepaid orders of large-print visit sheets, with their approval of the wording. We would print only after deposits cover paper, ink and delivery, and only if Sofia agrees the extra work fits the shop. In the first year after 2031, if code ends, we would continue only while repeat paid orders cover costs and a meaningful share of my lost wage, despite 2034 robots; otherwise I’d apply to real paid openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about code pay, but I can test an actual product without buying another machine. A stack of free large-print samples is a cost, not a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a care group need on the sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One carer said a medicine-time sheet needed space for a handwritten note. We would ask a care group to approve that layout before printing a paid batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the shop handle the extra orders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia’s shop would still handle its ordinary customers first. We would not promise care groups a delivery date that requires unpaid night work.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach code and design before 2034 robots.
I would test **prepaid large-print sheets** with care groups.
think: I expect my **code wage** could go when full thinking AI reaches routing software.
I cannot treat **free samples** as proof of paying demand from care groups.
do: **Seek** three prepaid care-group orders with wording approved.
**Print** only with Sofia’s agreement, deposits covering costs, and ordinary customers served before new care-group orders.
**Continue** if coding ends after 2031 only with repeat profitable orders replacing meaningful pay; avoid unpaid night work and apply otherwise.
feel: **Anxious** about lost pay, with a bounded paid-order test.
S3.quote: A stack of free large-print samples is a cost, not a business.
fieldNote: His **large-print trial** uses the existing press and requires approved wording, prepaid materials and Sofia’s consent.
Post-2031 **continuation** needs repeat net orders replacing meaningful wage despite approaching physical robots.

steps.text: Print prepaid sheets with Sofia’s agreement after costs and ordinary shop orders are covered
Continue after 2031 coding loss only with profitable repeats, meaningful pay and no unpaid nights
Apply to real paid openings if print demand fails after code loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 reaches dispatch code and print design in 2036; physical robots follow around 2039. A decade gives our union time to seek paid transitions and our household time to build real savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my job could still lose hours before 2036, and Sofia’s orders remain uneven today. Retirement is not a date I can promise with two weeks saved and no verified income statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking route failures with drivers and put 20 aside only on paydays after housing, food and paper. I’d join the workplace union’s transition group to seek paid training and report actual developer hours. In the first year after 2036, if code work ends, I’d apply to real paid openings; I would retire only if documented income and savings cover housing and shop obligations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the thin reserve despite ten years. Time is useful only if our wages and print orders let us save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would decide retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for our actual retirement statements and compare them with the mortgage balance. I will not treat the children’s incomes as an asset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you expand stock now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia and I would keep shop stock small until customers pay. A larger paper order on credit would make the reserve even thinner.

say: I expect **2036 AGI** to reach code and design before 2039 robots.
I would seek **paid transitions** through the workplace union.
think: I expect my **hours** could shrink before 2036.
I know **two weeks saved** cannot support an unverified retirement plan.
do: **Keep** driver-checked routes and save 20 only after household and paper bills.
**Join** union transition group to seek paid training and report actual hours.
**Apply** to real openings if code ends after 2036; retire only with verified resources.
feel: **Anxious** about current thin savings despite more warning.
S4.quote: A larger paper order on credit would make the reserve even thinner.
fieldNote: He combines **union action** with continued driver checks and tiny conditional savings.
The **retirement condition** includes documented income, mortgage and print-shop obligations without children’s wages.

steps.text: Keep checking route failures with drivers while employed
Save 20 only after housing, food and print-shop paper bills
Join union transition group for paid training and actual developer-hour reports
Apply to real paid openings if code ends after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because code pay and print design fees could fall before we build a month of savings. Written layoff terms, eligible help, real paid jobs and prepaid print orders would help. I would not ask the children to replace either income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the delivery driver whether the route ends at a door someone can open. A map can finish its trip while dinner is still outside.

headlineQuote: A map can finish its trip while dinner is still outside.
portrait: Ivan is a **58-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, low pay and two weeks saved.
He uses **AI daily** on delivery routes but checks driver notes, addresses and dispatcher reports.
His wife’s **print-shop orders** vary, exposing both code and design income to thinking AI.
He tests **prepaid large-print sheets** only with Sofia’s consent, covered materials and repeat paid demand.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce code pay and print-design fees before savings reach one month.
whatWouldHelp: **Written terms**, eligible help, real jobs and prepaid print orders would help.
